C01.note: Highest when the dusk signature, the code check of every night request against the merged orders, and the dark phone all run for real; this is the best answer to the hands-off theme. Lower if the night start through the Flows API fails or the model only drafts the list.

C02.note: The purest form of the house rule: the model gathers evidence, code sets the tag, and the model can only raise urgency. Higher if its evidence form drives the wake price (Reserve Price); lower if it is a code rule with a summary on top, and on stages.

C03.note: Visible model work (hypotheses, which mitigations to try) with code measuring each option on a no-traffic staging revision and a person tapping the tested one: a strong Assisted entry. Lower if replay cannot reproduce the failure or judges file it under incident root cause.

C04.note: Customer words become the alarm, a reproduction decides, and the gap gets a new monitor; Noor feeling believed is a real scene. Lower if Service Desk issues cannot start the flow and the schedule start is not accepted, or if the reproduction looks scripted.

C05.note: Owns what nobody owns today: the leftovers of the 3am response, with Sponge Count's opened 9, closed 8 as a crisp code check. Lower if flag, silence and scaling history is not readable by the flow token, so the mitigations look staged.

C06.note: Replay that must still catch every real incident is a good verifier, and the chart lands. Lower because the model's part could be a grid search (decoration) and weeks of metric and paging history must be seeded.

C07.note: Kind and practical, and Booster's weakened replay of a real past incident plus runbook fixes is a nice touch. Lower because it reads as an onboarding or training tool, and staged faults must feel real rather than toy.

C08.note: Warm idea with a great two-clock shot. Lower because the model only picks a helper, it touches two stages, and it needs time zones and status inside a flow, two real accounts, a night start and an outside timer.

C09.note: A sound rule (nothing risky moves while its people sleep), but code does almost everything, so the model is close to decoration, and days of rollout must be compressed on video.

C10.note: The model checking the expert's answer against the diff (rollback is not safe, 0042 drops a column) is exactly the visible capability I reward, and Ana's wedding is a real scene. Lower for overlap with organizational memory (LORE) and the need for a second account and user status.

C11.note: Real engineering: old code on the new schema, down migrations, checksums, and a written expand and contract split. Lower because the person is thin, it can look like another release gate, and schema history can eat days.

C12.note: The reporter gets the fix first, with consent, and her reply shapes the wider rollout while a person approves every widening: a user who feels heard. Lower if the story drifts into confirming the fix worked, which is Proof of Fix or the banned notifier.

C13.note: The clearest visible model capability in the pool: Claude completes a purchase using only what a screen reader announces, code decides success, and its only power is to hold. Lower if the browser cannot run in the flow and the journey degrades into a scripted test.

C14.note: Tests as proof: a test that passes on the old lockfile and fails on the new one is a real break, written from changelog lines nobody reads. Lower on wow and novelty, since dependency work sits next to the crowded security fixers and update bots.

C15.note: Safe hands-off (it can only keep images) on the rare package stage, but the model's share is thin and the human moment is a non-event that only a counterfactual can show.

C16.note: Builds and proves the escape hatch (flag-off path tested, staging toggle) before the night it is needed, and the 3am tap is a good scene. Lower because it works on the MR before merge, near code review agents, and auto-refactoring app code is risky.

C17.note: Good safety shape (code masks before the model sees anything) and deep Google Cloud use (Logging, Sensitive Data Protection). Lower because the person is a privacy lead, not a scene, and reading production logs after a release is the Proof of Fix mechanism.

C18.note: Complaints matched to a flag cohort by code is a signal nobody uses, and holding a step is the safe direction. Lower because it needs many believable seeded tickets and the statistic in the demo is thin.

C19.note: Automation that only moves between settings people wrote is a good principle. Lower because the model's role is small, approval rules and deploy freezes may need Maintainer, and the eight-day arc must be compressed.

C20.note: The line 'You said you'd revisit; here it is' is lovely. Lower because writing the proper fix is hard in general, the demo rests on one staged fix the agent gets right, and it overlaps Loose Ends.

C21.note: Funny and clear ('give me one reason to live'), with tests and a reference check proving a clean removal. Lower because flag cleanup tools exist outside the hackathon and the person feels little.

C22.note: The most original question in the pool: do our incident rituals work at all? Lower because it needs many incidents with metrics, small numbers often give no honest answer, and seeded history will look staged.

C23.note: Giving back upstream with a minimal reproduction shows real model skill and generosity. Lower because the upstream fix must arrive on cue (our own stand-in library) and the payoff is 21 days later.

C24.note: 'It is flaky, it is not you' is a good human line. Lower because retry statistics are code, the model only locates the failure, and flaky tests sit next to the excluded CI fixers.

C25.note: Agents learning only through skill files people approve is the right shape. Lower because GitLab already ships a Review instructions learner flow, and the demo needs other agents running and being corrected for days.

C26.note: Nobody handles leaving, and the finds are real GitLab facts checked by API (a schedule that runs as her stops when her account is blocked). Lower on wow, and reading other people's schedules and escalation policies may need Maintainer.

C27.note: Protects a person's 2am fix and writes it into code in her name; code decides drift and blocks the deploy, she decides keep or discard. Lower if Cloud Run config reads, audit logs and a non-human flow start cannot all be wired in time.

C28.note: Uses the model to make the human gate mean something, with a citation check in code: a real answer to approval fatigue. Lower because it is one step in one place, three stages, and the demo is a single quiet question.

C29.note: Turns the three autonomy levels into a path each action walks, granted by merge and revoked by code on a miss. Lower because the track record must be seeded, and judges may see it as another autonomy budget (BABYDOV).

C30.note: A nice moment for the author, but it lives next to Proof of Fix and June's Stayed Shipped, needs seven days of telemetry, and the model mostly writes prose around numbers code computed.

C31.note: Honest design (code computes, a person approves), but it sits beside the crowded evidence and attestation space, needs a quarter of history, and has almost no scene.

C32.note: Escrow until real traffic is zero is a clean rule for code, and the school librarian is a good person. Lower because the story takes weeks, so the video needs a compressed clock and several labelled fake callers.

C33.note: Every claim in the draft is checked against live state before support sees it, which is the right shape for a customer-facing agent. Lower because it sits close to the banned notifier and needs a full linked history across environments.

C34.note: The model thinks adversarially about data (apostrophes, accents, nulls) and writes probes, code runs the migration on a copy, and one broken name says it all. Lower on stages, and the synthetic dataset has to be good.

C35.note: Asking what would have to be true to remove a pin, at the moment of change, then checking it in code, is clever. Lower because the payoff is a staged one year later and turning free text into reliable checks is shaky.

C36.note: A failing test that code proves (fails with the change, passes without) plus a note a maintainer approves: kind, verified and human. Lower because the audience is narrow, and it needs a second account and an unverified revert trigger.

C37.note: Adversarial verification done right: plant a canary person, run the real deletion, and let code search every store, including ones the model found in this release. Lower if the app cannot hold several real stores; handle Laila's story with care.

C38.note: The best Assisted design: standby, go and hold, a cue-to-cue rehearsal on staging, and only a person says go. Lower on novelty, human pull and visible model work, and on video it can read as a release checklist.

C39.note: Turns the theme around: when a person needs the floor, every automation, other agents included, is locked in her name and a try-out proves it. Lower if deploy freezes, schedule pauses and trigger toggles need Maintainer in our project.

C40.note: An elegant autonomy boundary: alone while everything can be undone, a person at the first one-way step, floored by code rules. Lower because the person is thin and on video it risks looking like another release gatekeeper.

C41.note: Merged but undelivered work is a real gap. Lower because the work is mostly API queries and one mention, close to the stale merge request nudge bots, with little for the model to show.

C42.note: Checking a person's own understanding against live state is a good use of the model, and ownership moves only on a correct readback. Lower because it is the concept closest to the banned handoff notes and the in-flight list may not be readable.

C43.note: An agent that walks runbooks in staging and fixes the broken step shows real agentic skill inside a hard staging-only boundary. Lower because it needs a restorable backup and tight credentials, and turning prose into commands can wander.

C44.note: The customer marks the exact rows and code refuses anything unmarked (site mismatch: 11 rows, 1 marked): the best write-safety story in the pool. Lower on stages and sponsors, and the support story needs a second person.

C45.note: A missing production variable is a common outage, and the model never sees a secret (names and hashes only). Lower because it sits near release gating and the demo is a quiet table.

C46.note: Gloria's lost holidays are real, but counting performers needs months of history, the payoff is a month later, and it drifts toward onboarding aids.

C47.note: Shielding responders and replying personally to every user is kind. Lower because answering @shield ETA questions is one step from the excluded incident chatbot, and Service Desk setup is uncertain.

C48.note: Re-landing innocent changes one at a time finds the bad one by elimination, truth decided by code, and the row of MRs is a good visual. Lower because the model only orders the queue and several deploy cycles are slow to film.

C49.note: Finding the first future moment new code will meet (month end, a schedule, an expiry) is genuinely new reasoning. Lower because discovery must be general to convince and the person is thin.

C50.note: Starts from a business event, not a code change, with load tests as the truth and many stages touched. Lower because honest load testing on Cloud Run is fiddly and the payoff is a simulated Tuesday.

C51.note: Good safety design (a never-skip list in code, and the full pipeline runs right after). Lower because it is test selection under pressure, which CrossCut won with in June, and the demo needs a slow pipeline.

C52.note: One command freezes every change in motion, other agents included: a strong control story with a great visual. Lower because freezes likely need Maintainer and Lockout Tagout tells the same idea with a better person.

C53.note: Treating a retry as evidence is sharp, and a race that charges customers twice is a strong reveal. Lower because it needs an honest intermittent bug and hundreds of CI runs, and it lives next to CI failure fixers.

C54.note: Phases with a person's go and a no-blame note to the new hire who leaked the key: a good person and many stages. Lower because secret detection is crowded and real rotation needs a demo service whose keys we control.

C55.note: A real code to production hands-off loop on the developer's own terms. Lower because the model's judgment of soft conditions releases a deploy, which is power toward risk, and it sits next to auto-merge and gatekeepers.

C56.note: Code setting cooldowns from a rating is sensible. Lower because the model reads attacker-controlled changelogs and diffs whose rating can lead to an auto-merge, and dependency bots are well known.

C57.note: Asks who was hurt instead of why it broke, with code computing every credit and a person approving every message and repair. Lower because it needs believable accounts and incident data, and the demo is more table than scene.

top10.why: Hands-off with a fence: she signs tonight's reversible actions, code checks every request, and her phone stays dark; the best answer to how far agents can go without you.
Claude buys coffee using only what a screen reader announces; code decides success, its only power is to hold, and the audio lands in seconds.
Adversarial proof that deletion still deletes: a canary person is planted, deleted, and searched for by code in every store the model found.
The model gathers evidence, code decides whether to wake anyone, and the model can only add urgency: safe all-night autonomy that lets a parent sleep.
Turns the theme around: one person's lock stops every automation and agent, and a try-out proves it, so humans keep the floor.
Customer words become the alarm while monitors are green; a reproduction decides, and the gap gets a new monitor a person approves.
A 2am console fix is protected, written back in her name, and the next deploy refuses to erase it until she chooses.
Likely fixes are tested on staging before the half-awake engineer chooses: the model forms hypotheses, code measures, a person taps.
The model hunts for data shapes that break, code runs the migration on a copy, and one mangled name makes the risk human.
Changelog lines nobody reads become tests that pass on the old lockfile and fail on the new one: proof before merge for a weekend maintainer.

traps.why: Conditional trap shared with C02, C08 and C29: the 3am scene needs a non-human start (Flows API from a relay, or a person-owned schedule) to count as a human trigger, and paging needs Premium. Test it on day one or the core scene cannot be shown honestly.

Conditional trap: if a browser cannot run inside the flow and the journey falls back to a scripted Playwright test, the model becomes decoration and the concept collapses into a smoke test. Keep Claude choosing every key.

Framing trap: if the demo shows the reporter confirming the fix works, it is Proof of Fix with a new audience, and its sibling Promise Kept is the banned notifier. Keep the core on rollout order and consent.
Sits beside Proof of Fix and June's Stayed Shipped, needs seven days of real telemetry, and the model mostly narrates numbers code computed.
GitLab already ships a Review instructions learner flow, and the learning loop needs other agents running and corrected for days, so the demo is staged.
Evidence and attestation is a crowded space, a quarter of history must be generated, audit events may need Owner or Maintainer, and there is no scene.
Needs many past incidents with metrics; with small numbers the honest result is often unclear, and seeded history makes the statistics look staged.
Weeks of metric and paging history must be seeded, and the better rule could come from a grid search, so the model looks like decoration.
The model reads attacker-controlled changelogs and package diffs and its rating can lead to an auto-merge: a prompt injection path to production.
The model's judgment of soft conditions releases a production deploy, autonomy toward risk with a thin fence, and it depends on a schedule-started pipeline counting as a human trigger.
Code decides the window, the criteria and the percentage, so the model is decoration, and days of rollout must be compressed into the video.
Reading production logs after a release is the Proof of Fix mechanism with a new question, and the person is a privacy lead rather than a scene.
Answering ETA questions inside the incident is the excluded generic incident chatbot unless the outward personal replies are clearly the product.
CrossCut won June's Impact prize with CI test selection; judges may see an emergency version of the same thing.
